title: NURS 1017 Unit 5 Case Study 2
description: 8-year-old child presenting with facial honey-colored crusted impetigo and his 21-year-old sibling presenting with painful unilateral thoracic shingles, alongside clinical differentiation of cellulitis, syphilis, HSV-1, and fungal tinea infections.

question.stem: The nurse in a community family health clinic assesses 8-year-old Liam and his 21-year-old brother Marcus. Which clinical findings should the nurse recognize as hallmark cues of impetigo in Liam and herpes zoster (shingles) in Marcus? Select all that apply.

options.text: Liam: Erythematous vesicles and pustules around the mouth and nose that have ruptured to form thick, weeping golden-yellow 'honey-colored' crusts
Marcus: Unilateral crop of clustered, painful, tense vesicles on an erythematous base distributed along the right T6 dermatome of the chest and back
Marcus: Prodromal localized burning, itching, and severe sharp stabbing pain (hyperesthesia) in the right chest wall preceding the rash by 3 days
Liam: History of intense pruritus and scratching facial insect bites, with rapid spread of crusted lesions to his chin and cheeks
Bilateral symmetric silvery scaly plaques on the extensor elbows and knees with pitted fingernails
Diffuse generalized macular rash across both palms and soles accompanied by a painless genital ulcer (chancre)

question.explanation:
1. Impetigo (Liam): Highly contagious superficial bacterial infection (Staphylococcus aureus and/or Group A Streptococcus) typically presenting in children with vesicles that rupture, leaving weeping, exudative lesions with pathognomonic thick, golden-yellow 'honey-colored' crusts, exacerbated by scratching.
2. Herpes Zoster / Shingles (Marcus): Reactivation of latent Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) that has remained dormant in the dorsal root/neural ganglia since childhood chickenpox. It travels down a sensory nerve, manifesting as a dermatomal prodrome (burning, tingling, pain) followed by crops of vesicles on an erythematous base strictly confined to a unilateral dermatome.
3. Silvery plaques describe psoriasis. Palm/sole rash with painless chancre describes primary and secondary syphilis.

leftContent.intro: The nurse in an urgent care community health center is triaging Liam (8 years old) and his older brother Marcus (21 years old), brought in by their mother for acute dermatological complaints.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.content: 1000:Liam (8) and Marcus (21) present together. Liam: Mother notes Liam had mosquito bites on his chin 5 days ago; he scratched them persistently. Two days ago, small blisters appeared that burst and formed thick, sticky, yellowish-golden crusts that look like dried honey around his perioral area, nares, and chin. Lesions are weeping and itchy; child rubs face constantly. Vital signs: temp 37.1 °C, HR 92, RR 18. Marcus: 21-year-old college student; reports 4 days of severe burning, tingling, and deep aching pain along the right side of his mid-back and ribs. Yesterday morning, a crop of red bumps and clustered fluid-filled blisters erupted along that exact line. He states: 'Even my shirt brushing against my rib cage feels like fire.' Medical history: had chickenpox at age 4; no history of shingles. Physical exam confirms unilateral band-like vesicular eruption along right T6 dermatome, not crossing midline. Clear fluid in vesicles; no pustules or crusting yet. Nurse prepares infection control isolation and assessment.

question.stem: The nurse reviews common cutaneous infectious diseases encountered in clinical practice. For each clinical presentation, click to specify whether it represents a Bacterial Infection, a Viral Infection, or a Fungal / Yeast Infection.

rows.text: Acute superficial weeping vesicular infection developing honey-colored crusts caused by S. aureus or Group A Streptococcus (Impetigo)
Reactivation of latent virus in sensory dorsal root ganglia causing unilateral dermatomal vesicular eruption and intense neuralgic pain (Herpes Zoster)
Spreading, poorly demarcated deep dermal and subcutaneous erythema, localized heat, edema, and tenderness (Cellulitis)
Annular, ring-shaped erythematous plaque with elevated, scaly, vesicular advancing borders and central clearing on the trunk (Tinea Corporis)
Recurrent clusters of painful, fluid-filled vesicles around the lips and vermilion border preceded by tingling and burning (Herpes Simplex Type 1)
Painless indurated genital ulcer (chancre) occurring 2 to 6 weeks after sexual contact with Treponema pallidum (Primary Syphilis)

question.preamble: The nurse analyzes skin infection etiologies to prepare educational handouts (see Infectious Disease Matrix tab).
question.explanation:
1. Bacterial Infections: Impetigo (S. aureus/GAS; honey-colored crusts), Cellulitis (deep dermal/subcutaneous spreading infection caused by Streptococcus pyogenes or S. aureus), and Syphilis (Treponema pallidum spirochete; primary painless chancre, secondary palm/sole rash, tertiary neurosyphilis/gummas).
2. Viral Infections: Herpes Zoster (VZV reactivation along a dermatome), Herpes Simplex Virus 1 and 2 (cold sores/genital ulcers, latent in trigeminal/sacral ganglia), and Measles (rubeola; paramyxovirus with Koplik spots and morbilliform rash).
3. Fungal / Yeast Infections: Dermatophyte superficial mycoses (Tinea corporis [ringworm], Tinea pedis [athlete's foot], Tinea capitis, Tinea cruris) featuring annular scaly borders and central clearing; and Candida albicans (yeast infection presenting as oral thrush or intertrigo with satellite pustules).

leftContent.intro: The nurse conducts diagnostic sampling (bacterial swabs for Liam, viral PCR swab for Marcus) and reviews cutaneous infection categories.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.content: 1045:Swabs obtained: Liam's crusted facial lesion swabbed for bacterial culture and Gram stain; Marcus's vesicular fluid unroofed and swabbed for VZV PCR. Physical distancing and droplet/contact precautions maintained. Mother educated on the different causative organisms: bacteria for Liam (staph/strep) and virus for Marcus (shingles/varicella). Nurse reviews transmission precautions for both brothers.

tabs.title: Infectious Disease Matrix
tabs.content:
Diagnostic Investigations for Cutaneous Infections:
  • Bacterial Swabs: Gram stain and culture (Impetigo, Cellulitis exudate).
  • Blister Fluid PCR / Viral Culture: HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV (Zoster).
  • Skin Scrapings with KOH Mount / Fungal Culture: Tinea (hyphae and spores).
  • Serology (VDRL/RPR, Treponemal antibodies): Syphilis.
  • Wood's Lamp Fluorescence: Microsporum fungal tinea infections.

question.stem:
The nurse analyzes the pathophysiologic mechanisms of Varicella-Zoster Virus (VZV) latency and impetigo transmission.

Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

sentences: Following Marcus's childhood varicella (chickenpox) infection, the virus remained dormant in a latent state within the [drp1].
In managing Marcus's herpes zoster, the nurse recognizes that the primary clinical priority in an elderly or immunocompromised host is preventing [drp2].
For Liam's impetigo, the nurse instructs the mother that the condition is highly transmissible to others primarily via [drp3].

dropdowns.label: VZV latency site
options: sensory dorsal root or cranial nerve ganglia
subcutaneous adipose adipocytes
superficial keratinized stratum corneum cells
synovial fluid of large weight-bearing joints

dropdowns.label: zoster complication
options: postherpetic neuralgia (debilitating persistent neuropathic pain lasting months to years)
immediate systemic aplastic anemia and bone marrow fibrosis
acute full-thickness fourth-degree skin necrosis across the entire thorax
spontaneous malignant transformation into cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma

dropdowns.label: impetigo transmission route
options: direct contact with exudate, crusts, contaminated hands, or shared washcloths and towels
airborne droplet nuclei traveling across long distances through ventilation ducts
ingestion of undercooked poultry or unwashed root vegetables
transmission by domestic insect tick bites in wooded areas

question.explanation:
1. VZV Dormancy: After primary chickenpox, the varicella-zoster virus retrogradely ascends sensory nerves and resides indefinitely in a dormant state inside dorsal root ganglia or trigeminal sensory ganglia. Reactivation (triggered by stress, immunosuppression, or aging) causes the virus to migrate anterogradely down the sensory axon to the cutaneous dermatome.
2. Postherpetic Neuralgia (PHN): The most debilitating complication of shingles, characterized by severe intractable burning, stabbing neuropathic pain persisting > 90 days after rash resolution, caused by sensory nerve damage and chronic spinal cord sensitization.
3. Impetigo Transmission: Highly contagious bacterial pyoderma spread by direct skin-to-skin touch with open weeping sores or indirect contact via fomites (towels, washcloths, clothing, bed linen).

leftContent.intro: The nurse conducts detailed discharge counseling and infection control instruction with the mother and brothers.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.content: 1130:Preliminary results: Liam's Gram stain shows Gram-positive cocci in clusters and chains (Staphylococcus aureus and Streptococcus pyogenes). Marcus's VZV PCR confirmed positive. Oral valacyclovir and topical mupirocin 2% ointment ordered. Mother expresses concern: 'Can Marcus give Liam chickenpox or shingles? Can Liam give his little sister his face sores?' Nurse provides comprehensive infection control education regarding contact precautions and viral transmission.

question.stem: The nurse plans comprehensive nursing interventions and infection control protocols for Liam and Marcus. Which actions should the nurse include in the plan of care? Select all that apply.

options.text: Instruct Liam's mother to soak the facial crusts gently with warm water compresses to facilitate crust removal prior to applying prescribed topical mupirocin ointment
Emphasize strict separate laundering of Liam's and Marcus's towels, washcloths, and bed linens, and enforce meticulous hand hygiene after touching lesions
Instruct Marcus to keep his shingles vesicles completely covered with clean, non-stick dressings until all blisters have crusted over
Advise Marcus to strictly avoid contact with pregnant women who have not had chickenpox, unvaccinated infants, and immunocompromised individuals
Encourage Liam to attend elementary school immediately while weeping facial crusts are open and uncovered
Instruct Marcus to scratch and vigorously pop the shingles vesicles with a needle to relieve the burning nerve pain

question.explanation: Appropriate nursing care plans include: (1) Softening and gently removing impetigo crusts with warm compresses so topical mupirocin can penetrate directly into underlying infected tissue; (2) Strict fomite isolation (separate towels, linens) and frequent handwashing; (3) Keeping shingles lesions covered, which prevents transmission of VZV from vesicular fluid to susceptible people; and (4) Protecting non-immune individuals (pregnant women, infants, immunocompromised) because direct contact with shingles blister fluid can cause chickenpox in those without immunity. Children with active, draining impetigo should be excluded from school/daycare until 24 hours of effective antibiotic therapy has elapsed. Popping shingles vesicles risks secondary bacterial superinfection and does not relieve neuropathic pain.

leftContent.intro: The nurse organizes outpatient medication schedules, topical wound care, and contagion control strategies for both brothers.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.content: 1215:Nursing care plan established. Liam initiated on topical mupirocin 2% ointment TID after warm crust soaks; mother instructed to keep fingernails clipped short and clean to prevent scratching. Liam must remain home from school for 24 hours after starting antibiotics. Marcus initiated on oral valacyclovir 1,000 mg PO TID × 7 days, started within 72 hours of rash onset for optimal efficacy in reducing acute pain and preventing postherpetic neuralgia. Marcus provided hydrocolloid/gauze non-stick dressings to keep right flank lesions covered.

question.stem: The nurse evaluates planned clinical actions and topical therapies for cutaneous infections. For each nursing action, click to specify whether the intervention is Indicated, Non-Essential, or Contraindicated.

rows.text: Wash hands thoroughly with soap and water before and after applying topical antibiotic ointment to Liam's impetigo lesions
Apply high-potency topical fluorinated corticosteroid cream directly to Liam's open, weeping impetigo lesions
Administer prescribed oral valacyclovir on a consistent schedule and encourage adequate hydration to prevent renal tubular crystallization
Administer prescribed oral analgesics (acetaminophen, NSAIDs, or neuropathic agents) to manage Marcus's sharp shingles pain
Perform continuous 12-lead electrocardiographic monitoring for Liam in the clinic setting
Allow Liam and Marcus to share bathwater and facial towels during acute active blistering

question.preamble: Clinical management and infection control execution in urgent care.
question.explanation:
1. Indicated: Rigorous hand hygiene prevents autoinoculation and spread of S. aureus/Streptococcus to other body sites or household members.
2. Contraindicated: Topical corticosteroids suppress local cutaneous immune responses and are contraindicated in active untreated bacterial, viral, or fungal infections, as they cause worsening proliferation.
3. Indicated: Oral valacyclovir/acyclovir is excreted renally; maintaining good hydration prevents drug crystallization in renal tubules.
4. Indicated: Controlling acute shingles pain improves mobility, sleep, and decreases chronic neural sensitization.
5. Non-Essential: Continuous 12-lead ECG monitoring is unnecessary for uncomplicated pediatric impetigo.
6. Contraindicated: Sharing bathwater or towels promotes immediate cross-transmission of both bacterial and viral pathogens.

leftContent.intro: The nurse reviews medication administration, expected healing timelines, and infection resolution markers with Marcus and Liam's mother.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.content: 1300:Prescriptions reviewed and dispensed. First dose of oral valacyclovir taken by Marcus with a large glass of water. Liam's mother demonstrated proper technique for soaking crusts and applying thin layer of mupirocin ointment with a cotton swab. Mother agrees to keep Liam home until tomorrow afternoon when 24 hours of treatment is completed. Follow-up scheduled in 1 week.

question.stem:
The nurse evaluates client and family comprehension prior to discharge from the clinic.

Complete the following sentences by choosing from the lists of options.

sentences: The nurse recognizes that Marcus understands shingles transmission when he states that an unvaccinated person exposed to his open blister fluid could develop [drp1].
In evaluating Liam's progress, the nurse instructs the mother to monitor for systemic complications and contact the healthcare provider immediately if Liam develops [drp2].
To prevent future recurrent episodes of shingles, the nurse educates Marcus that after full recovery, older adults and at-risk individuals should receive [drp3].

dropdowns.label: transmission risk
options: chickenpox (varicella), not shingles directly
immediate systemic syphilis with palmar rash
impetigo with golden-yellow crusting
a superficial tinea fungal ringworm lesion

dropdowns.label: impetigo complication
options: periorbital edema, dark cola-colored urine, and hypertension (post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis)
sudden severe loss of deep tendon reflexes and foot drop
widespread silvery plaques over extensor joints
acute paraneoplastic hypercalcemia and polyuria

dropdowns.label: zoster prevention
options: the recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) to boost VZV-specific cell-mediated immunity
lifelong daily prophylactic penicillin injections
annual immunization with the trivalent oral polio vaccine
daily application of topical antifungal creams

question.explanation:
1. Shingles Transmission Truth: Shingles cannot be caught directly as shingles from another person. The vesicular fluid contains active VZV; if an individual who is non-immune (never had chickenpox and never vaccinated) comes into direct contact with the blister fluid, they will contract primary Varicella (chickenpox).
2. Post-Streptococcal Glomerulonephritis (PSGN): Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus causing impetigo can lead to immune-complex mediated PSGN 1 to 3 weeks later. Warning signs include periorbital edema, dark tea- or cola-colored urine (hematuria), oliguria, and hypertension.
3. Shingrix Immunization: Recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) is highly effective (> 90%) in boosting waning VZV cell-mediated immunity in adults 50+ (or immunocompromised 19+), preventing shingles reactivation and postherpetic neuralgia.

leftContent.intro: Liam and Marcus complete their clinic visit and receive written infection control and disease recovery summaries.

tabs.title: Nurses' Notes
tabs.content: 1330:Final discharge debriefing concluded. Mother verbalized signs of post-streptococcal nephritis (facial puffiness, tea-colored urine) requiring medical re-evaluation for Liam. Marcus stated he will avoid his pregnant sister-in-law until his blisters are completely crusted and dry. Both clients expressed satisfaction with the care and clear understanding of the pathophysiology.
